avoidRenderBlocking.advice: The page has 3 blocking requests and 0 in body parser blocking (1 JavaScript and 2 CSS).
avoidRenderBlocking.description: The critical rendering path is what the browser needs to do to start rendering the page. Every file requested inside of the head element will postpone the rendering of the page, because the browser need to do the request. Avoid loading JavaScript synchronously inside of the head (you should not need JavaScript to render the page), request files from the same domain as the main document (to avoid DNS lookups) and inline CSS for really fast rendering and a short rendering path.
avoidRenderBlocking.title: Avoid slowing down the critical rendering path

avoidScalingImages.advice: The page has 13 images that are scaled more than 100 pixels. It would be better if those images are sent so the browser don't need to scale them.
avoidScalingImages.description: It's easy to scale images in the browser and make sure they look good in different devices, however that is bad for performance! Scaling images in the browser takes extra CPU time and will hurt performance on mobile. And the user will download extra kilobytes (sometimes megabytes) of data that could be avoided. Don't do that, make sure you create multiple version of the same image server-side and serve the appropriate one.
avoidScalingImages.title: Don't scale images in the browser

cssPrint.description: Loading a specific stylesheet for printing slows down the page, even though it is not used. You can include the print styles inside your other CSS file(s) just by using an @media query targeting type print.

decodingAsync.advice: The page has 16 images (out of 28) without a decoding hint. Add decoding="async" to non-critical images so the browser can decode them off the main thread.
decodingAsync.description: Setting decoding="async" on an tells the browser it can decode the image off the main thread, which keeps the page responsive to user interactions while images are being processed. The default ("auto") leaves the choice to the browser. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/img#decoding
decodingAsync.title: Add decoding="async" to non-critical images

firstContentfulPaint.advice: First contentful paint is poor (3.692 s). It is in the Google Web Vitals poor range, slower than 3 seconds.
firstContentfulPaint.description: The First Contentful Paint (FCP) metric measures the time from when the page starts loading to when any part of the page content is rendered on the screen. For this metric, "content" refers to text, images (including background images), <svg> elements, or non-white <canvas> elements.
firstContentfulPaint.title: Have a fast first contentful paint

googleTagManager.advice: The page is using Google Tag Manager, this is a performance risk since non-tech users can add JavaScript to your page.
googleTagManager.description: Google Tag Manager makes it possible for non tech users to add scripts to your page that will downgrade performance.
googleTagManager.title: Avoid using Google Tag Manager.

inlineCss.advice: The page has both inline CSS and CSS requests even though it uses a HTTP/2-ish connection. If you have many users on slow connections, it can be better to only inline the CSS. Run your own tests and check the waterfall graph to see what happens.
inlineCss.description: In the early days of the Internet, inlining CSS was one of the ugliest things you can do. That has changed if you want your page to start rendering fast for your user. Always inline the critical CSS when you use HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (avoid doing CSS requests that block rendering) and lazy load and cache the rest of the CSS. It is a little more complicated when using HTTP/2. Does your server support HTTP push? Then maybe that can help. Do you have a lot of users on a slow connection and are serving large chunks of HTML? Then it could be better to use the inline technique, becasue some servers always prioritize HTML content over CSS so the user needs to download the HTML first, before the CSS is downloaded.
inlineCss.title: Inline CSS for faster first render

interactionToNextPaint.advice: No interactions were observed during this page load, so Interaction to Next Paint cannot be assessed in this snapshot. INP is best measured with real-user monitoring.
interactionToNextPaint.description: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) is one of the Google Core Web Vitals — it replaced First Input Delay in March 2024 — and measures the latency of the slowest interaction with the page. To be fast according to Google, the p75 across all interactions should be under 200 ms, and over 500 ms is poor performance. INP is best measured with real-user monitoring; this rule reports what it can observe from the events that happened during the test.
interactionToNextPaint.title: Have a fast Interaction to Next Paint

jquery.description: There are sites out there that use multiple versions of jQuery on the same page. You shouldn't do that because the user will then unnecessarily download extra data. Cleanup the code and make sure you only use one version.

largestContentfulPaint.advice: Largest contentful paint is poor 6.840 s. It is in the Google Web Vitals poor range, slower than 4 seconds.
largestContentfulPaint.description: Largest contentful paint is one of Google Web Vitals and reports the render time of the largest image or text block visible within the viewport, relative to when the page first started loading. To be fast according to Google, it needs to render before 2.5 seconds and results over 4 seconds is poor performance.
largestContentfulPaint.title: Have a fast largest contentful paint

lazyLoadingImages.advice: The page has 6 below-the-fold images without loading="lazy". Add loading="lazy" so the browser defers downloading and decoding them until the user scrolls them into view.
lazyLoadingImages.description: Adding loading="lazy" to an tells the browser not to download or decode it until it is close to the viewport. For images that the user may never see (deep in the page, behind a tab, in a footer carousel), this saves bandwidth and main-thread time during initial render. The LCP image and any image in the initial viewport should NOT be lazy-loaded — that delays the first paint. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/img#loading
lazyLoadingImages.title: Lazy-load below-the-fold images

lcpImageHints.advice: The LCP element is not an image, so this rule does not apply.
lcpImageHints.description: When the Largest Contentful Paint element is an image, the browser priority hints applied to that element directly affect the LCP metric. The image must NOT be loading="lazy" (that defers the fetch until near-viewport, which is the opposite of what an LCP image needs) and SHOULD be fetchpriority="high" (so the browser fetches it with high priority instead of guessing). https://web.dev/articles/fetch-priority
lcpImageHints.title: Apply the right priority hints to the LCP image

longTasks.advice: The page has 20 CPU long tasks with the total of 3.029 s. The total blocking time is 1.393 s  and 5 long tasks before first contentful paint with total time of 886 ms. longTasks.description: Long CPU tasks locks the thread. To the user this is commonly visible as a "locked up" page where the browser is unable to respond to user input; this is a major source of bad user experience on the web today. However the CPU Long Task is depending on the computer/phones actual CPU speed, so you should measure this on the same type of the device that your user is using. To debug you should use the Chrome timeline log and drag/drop it into devtools or use Firefox Geckoprofiler.

modernImageFormats.advice: The page ships 11 images (out of 23) in JPEG/PNG/GIF without a modern alternative. Wrap them in a with a or "image/webp" before the legacy , or serve modern formats from your image pipeline directly. AVIF and WebP usually deliver 25–50% smaller files at the same quality.
modernImageFormats.description: AVIF and WebP routinely deliver 25–50% smaller files than JPEG and PNG at the same perceived quality, and every browser version still under support understands at least one of them. Ship modern formats either through a element with / "image/webp" entries in front of the legacy , or directly from a content-negotiating image pipeline that returns AVIF / WebP when the client accepts it. https://web.dev/articles/serve-images-webp
modernImageFormats.title: Serve images in modern formats (AVIF, WebP)

spof.advice: The page has 1 request inside of the head that can cause a SPOF (single point of failure). Load them asynchronously or move them outside of the document head.
spof.description: A page can be stopped from loading in the browser if a single JavaScript, CSS, and in some cases a font, couldn't be fetched or is loading really slowly (the white screen of death). That is a scenario you really want to avoid. Never load 3rd-party components synchronously inside of the head tag.
spof.title: Avoid Frontend single point of failures

cacheHeaders.title: Avoid extra requests by setting cache headers
cacheHeaders.description: The easiest way to make your page fast is to avoid doing requests to the server. Setting a cache header on your server response will tell the browser that it doesn't need to download the asset again during the configured cache time! Always try to set a cache time if the content doesn't change for every request.
cacheHeaders.advice: The page has 214 requests that are missing a cache time. Configure a cache time so the browser doesn't need to download them every time. It will save 2 MB the next access.

cacheHeadersLong.title: Long cache headers is good
cacheHeadersLong.description: Setting a cache header is good. Setting a long cache header (a year) is even better because the asset will stay in the browser cache across visits. For content-hashed URLs (e.g. app.4af2.css) you can safely use Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. For unversioned URLs that may change, use a revalidating strategy instead.
cacheHeadersLong.advice: The page has 35 requests that have a shorter cache time than one year (but still a cache time).

compressAssets.title: Always compress text content
compressAssets.description: In the early days of the Internet there were browsers that didn't support compressing (gzipping) text content. They do now. Make sure you compress HTML, JSON, JavaScript, CSS and SVG. It will save bytes for the user; making the page load faster and use less bandwith.

connectionKeepAlive.title: Don't close a connection that is used multiple times

There has been some hacks in the past that suggested closing the connection as fast as possible in order to create new ones, but that shouldn't be applicable anymore.

ga.description: Google Analytics share private user information with Google that your user hasn't agreed on sharing.

referrerPolicy.advice: No <meta name="referrer"> tag was found on the page. Set a Referrer-Policy response header (preferred) or add a meta tag, for example <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">.

Set a Referrer-Policy response header (preferred) or a <meta name="referrer"> tag in the document. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy
referrerPolicy.title: Declare a referrer policy on the document

sessionReplay.description: Session-replay tools (Hotjar, FullStory, Microsoft Clarity, LogRocket, Smartlook, Mouseflow and similar) record user behaviour on the page in detail. They have legitimate uses but they have also been shown to capture personally-identifiable information from form fields when not configured with redaction. If you use one of these, make sure input redaction is on, that you have explicit user consent under the relevant regulation (GDPR, CCPA, etc.) before recording starts, and that you know where the recordings are stored and for how long. https://www.princeton.edu/~jmayer/papers/Acar2018.pdf
sessionReplay.title: Configure session-replay tools carefully if you use them

surveillance.advice: The page embeds 7 resources from companies that profit from user surveillance. Consider privacy-respecting alternatives.
surveillance.description: Embedding scripts or iframes from companies whose business model is surveillance capitalism (Google, Facebook, etc.) leaks detailed user data on every page view, often before the user has had a chance to consent. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance_capitalism for background. Prefer privacy-respecting alternatives where possible.
surveillance.title: Avoid embedding services from surveillance capitalist companies

youtube.description: If you include Youtube videos on your page, you are sharing private user information with Google.
youtube.title: Avoid including Youtube videos

contentSecurityPolicyHeader.title: Use a strict Content-Security-Policy header to mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.description: A Content-Security-Policy response header tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed. The most effective form is a strict CSP using nonces or hashes together with strict-dynamic; the worst is a missing header, with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval close behind. https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.advice: The policy declares no default-src or script-src directive, which means scripts can be loaded from anywhere. Add at least default-src so unknown directive types fall back to a safe value. contentSecurityPolicyHeader.title: Use a strict Content-Security-Policy header to mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.description: A Content-Security-Policy response header tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed. The most effective form is a strict CSP using nonces or hashes together with strict-dynamic; the worst is a missing header, with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval close behind. https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.advice: The policy declares no default-src or script-src directive, which means scripts can be loaded from anywhere. crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header so cross-origin subresources opt in to being embedded.
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) makes the page refuse to load cross-origin subresources unless they explicitly opt in via CORP or CORS. Together with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header (typically require-corp or credentialless) on the document response to control cross-origin embedding.

crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) lets a page sever its window-group ties to cross-origin documents that opened it or that it opens. Together with Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header (typically same-origin) on the document response to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.

crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header to limit who may embed the page.
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP) is a per-response opt-in that tells the browser which origins are allowed to embed the resource. It blocks cross-origin or cross-site no-cors embedding (img, script, iframe, etc.) and is one of the building blocks of cross-origin isolation. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header (same-origin, same-site or cross-origin) on the document response to limit who may embed it.

nelHeader.title: Set a NEL header so the browser reports network errors back to you.

Together they give you visibility into errors that never reach your origin server. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/NEL
nelHeader.advice: Set a NEL header (paired with Reporting-Endpoints) to collect connection-level error reports from the field.

permissionsPolicyHeader.title: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.

permissionsPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.

referrerPolicyHeader.title: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.

reportingEndpointsHeader.title: Declare reporting endpoints so the browser can deliver Reporting-API events.

inlineCss.description: In the early days of the Internet, inlining CSS was one of the ugliest things you can do. That has changed if you want your page to start rendering fast for your user. Always inline the critical CSS when you use HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (avoid doing CSS requests that block rendering) and lazy load and cache the rest of the CSS. It is a little more complicated when using HTTP/2. Does your server support HTTP push? Then maybe that can help. Do you have a lot of users on a slow connection and are serving large chunks of HTML? Then it could be better to use the inline technique, becasue some servers always prioritize HTML content over CSS so the user needs to download the HTML first, before the CSS is downloaded.

However the CPU Long Task is depending on the computer/phones actual CPU speed, so you should measure this on the same type of the device that your user is using. longTasks.title: Avoid CPU Long Tasks

modernImageFormats.advice: The page ships 12 images (out of 24) in JPEG/PNG/GIF without a modern alternative. Wrap them in a with a or "image/webp" before the legacy , or serve modern formats from your image pipeline directly. AVIF and WebP usually deliver 25–50% smaller files at the same quality.
modernImageFormats.description: AVIF and WebP routinely deliver 25–50% smaller files than JPEG and PNG at the same perceived quality, and every browser version still under support understands at least one of them. Ship modern formats either through a element with / "image/webp" entries in front of the legacy , or directly from a content-negotiating image pipeline that returns AVIF / WebP when the client accepts it. https://web.dev/articles/serve-images-webp
modernImageFormats.title: Serve images in modern formats (AVIF, WebP)

spof.advice: The page has 1 request inside of the head that can cause a SPOF (single point of failure). Load them asynchronously or move them outside of the document head.
spof.description: A page can be stopped from loading in the browser if a single JavaScript, CSS, and in some cases a font, couldn't be fetched or is loading really slowly (the white screen of death). That is a scenario you really want to avoid. Never load 3rd-party components synchronously inside of the head tag.
spof.title: Avoid Frontend single point of failures

assetsRedirects.title: Avoid doing redirects
assetsRedirects.description: A redirect is one extra step for the user to download the asset. Avoid that if you want to be fast. Redirects are even more of a showstopper on mobile.
assetsRedirects.advice: The page has 1 redirect. 1 request are from other domains, it could be 3rd-party assets doing unnecessary redirects. :(

cacheHeaders.title: Avoid extra requests by setting cache headers
cacheHeaders.description: The easiest way to make your page fast is to avoid doing requests to the server. Setting a cache header on your server response will tell the browser that it doesn't need to download the asset again during the configured cache time! Always try to set a cache time if the content doesn't change for every request.
cacheHeaders.advice: The page has 203 requests that are missing a cache time. Configure a cache time so the browser doesn't need to download them every time. It will save 2 MB the next access.

cacheHeadersLong.title: Long cache headers is good
cacheHeadersLong.description: Setting a cache header is good. Setting a long cache header (a year) is even better because the asset will stay in the browser cache across visits. For content-hashed URLs (e.g. app.4af2.css) you can safely use Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. For unversioned URLs that may change, use a revalidating strategy instead.
cacheHeadersLong.advice: The page has 35 requests that have a shorter cache time than one year (but still a cache time).

compressAssets.title: Always compress text content
compressAssets.description: In the early days of the Internet there were browsers that didn't support compressing (gzipping) text content. They do now. Make sure you compress HTML, JSON, JavaScript, CSS and SVG. It will save bytes for the user; making the page load faster and use less bandwith.
compressAssets.advice: The page has 4 requests that are served uncompressed. You could save a lot of bytes by sending them compressed instead.

connectionKeepAlive.title: Don't close a connection that is used multiple times
connectionKeepAlive.description: Use keep-alive headers and don't close the connection when we have multiple requests to the same domain. There has been some hacks in the past that suggested closing the connection as fast as possible in order to create new ones, but that shouldn't be applicable anymore.

cpuTimeSpentInRendering.title: Avoid spend too much CPU time to render the page
cpuTimeSpentInRendering.description: You need to be able to render the page fast. This metric depends on which computer/device you run on but the limit here is high: Spending more time than 500 ms will alert this advice.
cpuTimeSpentInRendering.advice: We can only get CPU spent time if you use Chrome to test the page.

cpuTimeSpentInScripting.title: Avoid executing too much JavaScript
cpuTimeSpentInScripting.description: Do not run too much JavaSript, that will slow down the page for your user. This metric depends on which computer/device you run on but the limit here is high: Spending more time than 1000 ms will alert this advice
cpuTimeSpentInScripting.advice: We can only get CPU spent time if you use Chrome to test the page.

cssSize.title: Total CSS size shouldn't be too big
cssSize.description: Delivering a massive amount of CSS to the browser is not the best thing you can do, because it means more work for the browser when parsing the CSS against the HTML and that makes the rendering slower. Try to send only the CSS that is used on that page. And make sure to remove CSS rules when they aren't used anymore.
cssSize.advice: The total CSS transfer size is 159 kB and uncompressed size is 1.1 MB. That is big and the CSS could most probably be smaller.

documentRedirect.title: Avoid redirecting the main document
documentRedirect.description: You should never ever redirect the main document, because it will make the page load slower for the user. Well, you should redirect the user if the user tries to use HTTP and there's an HTTPS version of the page. The coach checks for that. :)

favicon.title: The favicon should be small and cacheable
favicon.description: It is easy to make the favicon big but please avoid doing that, because every browser will then perform an unnecessarily large download. And make sure the cache headers are set for a long time for the favicon. It is easy to miss since it's another content type.
favicon.advice: The favicon size is 26.6 kB bytes. That's quite big, can you make it smaller? The favicon has no cache time.

fewFonts.title: Avoid too many fonts
fewFonts.description: How many fonts do you need on a page for the user to get the message? Fonts can slow down the rendering of content, try to avoid loading too many of them because worst case it can make the text invisible until they are loaded (FOIT—flash of invisible text), best case they will flicker the text content when they arrive.
fewFonts.advice: The page has 5 font requests. Do you really need them? What value does the fonts give the user?

fewRequestsPerDomain.title: Avoid too many requests per domain [HTTP/1]
fewRequestsPerDomain.description: Browsers have a limit on how many concurrent requests they can do per domain when using HTTP/1. When you hit the limit, the browser will wait before it can download more assets on that domain. So avoid having too many requests per domain.
fewRequestsPerDomain.advice: There are almost no limits on HTTP/2 connections with the number of requests, but that is not completely true. It depends on how they are downloaded. Please check your HAR file, does it look OK?

headerSize.title: Response headers should't be too big [HTTP/1]
headerSize.description: Avoid a lot of cookies and other stuff that makes your headers big when you use HTTP/1 because the headers are not compressed. You will send extra data to the user.

imageSize.title: Total image size shouldn't be too big
imageSize.description: Avoid having too many large images on the page. The images will not affect the first paint of the page, but it will eat bandwidth for the user.

javascriptSize.title: Total JavaScript size shouldn't be too big
javascriptSize.description: A lot of JavaScript often means you are downloading more than you need. How complex is the page and what can the user do on the page? Do you use multiple JavaScript frameworks?
javascriptSize.advice: The total JavaScript transfer size is 2.8 MB and the uncompressed size is 8.6 MB. This is totally crazy! There is really room for improvement here.

mimeTypes.title: Avoid using incorrect mime types
mimeTypes.description: It's not a great idea to let browsers guess content types (content sniffing), in some cases it can actually be a security risk.
mimeTypes.advice: The page has 1 misconfigured mime type.

optimalCssSize.title: Make each CSS response small
optimalCssSize.description: Render-blocking CSS holds up the first paint until it has fully downloaded, parsed and applied, so smaller CSS files mean a faster start. Split your CSS into a small critical bundle inlined or eagerly loaded, with the rest lazy-loaded.
optimalCssSize.advice: https://www.home-appliances.philips/styles-NAEYIIOD.css size is 146.3 kB (146293) and that is bigger than the limit of 25 kB. Try to keep each CSS response under 25 kB.

pageSize.title: Total page size shouldn't be too big
pageSize.description: Avoid having pages that have a transfer size over the wire of more than 3 MB (desktop) and 2 MB (mobile) because heavy pages hurt performance and are expensive for users on metered connections. Reference: HTTP Archive median page weight in 2024 was around 2.7 MB desktop / 2.4 MB mobile, so this rule fires when a page is above the modern median.
pageSize.advice: The page total transfer size is 3.9 MB, which is more than the coach limit of 3 MB. That is really big and you need to make it smaller.

privateAssets.title: Don't use private headers on static content
privateAssets.description: If you set private headers on content, that means that the content are specific for that user. Static content should be able to be cached and used by everyone. Avoid setting the cache header to private.
privateAssets.advice: The page has 16 requests with private headers. Make sure that the assets really should be private and only used by one user. Otherwise, make it cacheable for everyone.

responseOk.title: Avoid missing and error requests
responseOk.description: Your page should never request assets that return a 400 or 500 error. These requests are never cached. If that happens something is broken. Please fix it.

fingerprint.description: Fingerprinting consists of collecting different kinds of information about the user with the goal of building a unique "fingerprint" for them. Different types of fingerprinting are used on the web by trackers. Browser fingerprinting use characteristics specific to the browser of the user, relying on the fact that the chance of another user having the exact same browser set-up is fairly small if there are a large enough number of variables to track
fingerprint.title: Do not fingerprint your user.

iframeSandbox.description: Adding a sandbox attribute to a cross-origin iframe restricts what the embedded page can do (script execution, form submission, top-level navigation, popups, etc.) and is one of the cheapest ways to limit the blast radius of a third-party embed. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/iframe#sandbox
iframeSandbox.title: Sandbox cross-origin iframes

referrerPolicy.advice: No <meta name="referrer"> tag was found on the page. Set a Referrer-Policy response header (preferred) or add a meta tag, for example <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">.
referrerPolicy.description: Without an explicit referrer policy the browser falls back to the user-agent default and may leak the full URL of the previous page (including query strings) to every cross-origin request. Set a Referrer-Policy response header (preferred) or a <meta name="referrer"> tag in the document. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy
referrerPolicy.title: Declare a referrer policy on the document

sessionReplay.description: Session-replay tools (Hotjar, FullStory, Microsoft Clarity, LogRocket, Smartlook, Mouseflow and similar) record user behaviour on the page in detail. They have legitimate uses but they have also been shown to capture personally-identifiable information from form fields when not configured with redaction. If you use one of these, make sure input redaction is on, that you have explicit user consent under the relevant regulation (GDPR, CCPA, etc.) before recording starts, and that you know where the recordings are stored and for how long. https://www.princeton.edu/~jmayer/papers/Acar2018.pdf
sessionReplay.title: Configure session-replay tools carefully if you use them

surveillance.advice: The page embeds 6 resources from companies that profit from user surveillance. Consider privacy-respecting alternatives.

surveillance.title: Avoid embedding services from surveillance capitalist companies

youtube.description: If you include Youtube videos on your page, you are sharing private user information with Google.

contentSecurityPolicyHeader.title: Use a strict Content-Security-Policy header to mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.description: A Content-Security-Policy response header tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed. The most effective form is a strict CSP using nonces or hashes together with strict-dynamic; the worst is a missing header, with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval close behind. https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.advice: The policy declares no default-src or script-src directive, which means scripts can be loaded from anywhere. Add at least default-src so unknown directive types fall back to a safe value. Set object-src 'none' (or a default-src 'none' fallback) so the page cannot load Flash, plugins or other legacy embeddable content.

crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header so cross-origin subresources opt in to being embedded.
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) makes the page refuse to load cross-origin subresources unless they explicitly opt in via CORP or CORS. Together with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header (typically require-corp or credentialless) on the document response to control cross-origin embedding.

crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) lets a page sever its window-group ties to cross-origin documents that opened it or that it opens. Together with Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header (typically same-origin) on the document response to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.

crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header to limit who may embed the page.
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP) is a per-response opt-in that tells the browser which origins are allowed to embed the resource. It blocks cross-origin or cross-site no-cors embedding (img, script, iframe, etc.) and is one of the building blocks of cross-origin isolation. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header (same-origin, same-site or cross-origin) on the document response to limit who may embed it.

googleReCaptcha.title: Avoid using Google reCAPTCHA
googleReCaptcha.description: You should avoid using Google reCAPTCHA since it will share your users information with Google.

mixedContent.title: Serve all responses on HTTPS (when you are on HTTPS)
mixedContent.description: You need to make sure that if you are on HTTPS, all responses are on HTTPS so that the content served are secured.

nelHeader.title: Set a NEL header so the browser reports network errors back to you.
nelHeader.description: The NEL (Network Error Logging) response header tells the browser to record connection-level failures (DNS, TLS, HTTP errors) and ship them to a reporting endpoint. NEL pairs with the Reporting-Endpoints / Report-To header — the page declares the endpoint group and NEL points at it. Together they give you visibility into errors that never reach your origin server. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/NEL
nelHeader.advice: Set a NEL header (paired with Reporting-Endpoints) to collect connection-level error reports from the field.

permissionsPolicyHeader.title: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.
permissionsPolicyHeader.description: The Permissions-Policy response header (the successor to Feature-Policy) lets a site explicitly opt in or out of powerful browser features such as camera, microphone, geolocation, payment and clipboard. Setting a strict policy reduces the attack surface and limits what embedded third parties can do. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Permissions-Policy
permissionsPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.

referrerPolicyHeader.title: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.
referrerPolicyHeader.description: Referrer Policy is a new header that allows a site to control how much information the browser includes with navigations away from a document and should be set by all sites. https://scotthelme.co.uk/a-new-security-header-referrer-policy/.
referrerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.

reportingEndpointsHeader.title: Declare reporting endpoints so the browser can deliver Reporting-API events.
reportingEndpointsHeader.description: The Reporting-Endpoints response header (the successor to Report-To) names the URLs that browsers should POST reports to. Without it, CSP report-to directives, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have nowhere to go. The legacy Report-To header is still accepted for older Chromium versions. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Reporting-Endpoints
reportingEndpointsHeader.advice: Set a Reporting-Endpoints header (or the legacy Report-To header) so CSP reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have an endpoint to land at.

strictTransportSecurityHeader.title: Set a strict transport header to make sure the user always use HTTPS.
strictTransportSecurityHeader.description: The HTTP Strict-Transport-Security response header (often abbreviated as HSTS) lets a web site tell browsers that it should only be accessed using HTTPS, instead of using HTTP. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security.

avoidRenderBlocking.advice: The page has 3 blocking requests and 0 in body parser blocking (1 JavaScript and 2 CSS).
avoidRenderBlocking.description: The critical rendering path is what the browser needs to do to start rendering the page. Every file requested inside of the head element will postpone the rendering of the page, because the browser need to do the request. Avoid loading JavaScript synchronously inside of the head (you should not need JavaScript to render the page), request files from the same domain as the main document (to avoid DNS lookups) and inline CSS for really fast rendering and a short rendering path.
avoidRenderBlocking.title: Avoid slowing down the critical rendering path

avoidScalingImages.advice: The page has 13 images that are scaled more than 100 pixels. It would be better if those images are sent so the browser don't need to scale them.
avoidScalingImages.description: It's easy to scale images in the browser and make sure they look good in different devices, however that is bad for performance! Scaling images in the browser takes extra CPU time and will hurt performance on mobile. And the user will download extra kilobytes (sometimes megabytes) of data that could be avoided. Don't do that, make sure you create multiple version of the same image server-side and serve the appropriate one.
avoidScalingImages.title: Don't scale images in the browser

decodingAsync.description: Setting decoding="async" on an tells the browser it can decode the image off the main thread, which keeps the page responsive to user interactions while images are being processed. The default ("auto") leaves the choice to the browser. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/img#decoding
decodingAsync.title: Add decoding="async" to non-critical images

firstContentfulPaint.advice: First contentful paint is poor (3.560 s). It is in the Google Web Vitals poor range, slower than 3 seconds.
firstContentfulPaint.description: The First Contentful Paint (FCP) metric measures the time from when the page starts loading to when any part of the page content is rendered on the screen. For this metric, "content" refers to text, images (including background images), <svg> elements, or non-white <canvas> elements.
firstContentfulPaint.title: Have a fast first contentful paint

googleTagManager.advice: The page is using Google Tag Manager, this is a performance risk since non-tech users can add JavaScript to your page.

inlineCss.advice: The page has both inline CSS and CSS requests even though it uses a HTTP/2-ish connection. If you have many users on slow connections, it can be better to only inline the CSS. Run your own tests and check the waterfall graph to see what happens.
inlineCss.description: In the early days of the Internet, inlining CSS was one of the ugliest things you can do. That has changed if you want your page to start rendering fast for your user. Always inline the critical CSS when you use HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (avoid doing CSS requests that block rendering) and lazy load and cache the rest of the CSS. It is a little more complicated when using HTTP/2. Does your server support HTTP push? Then maybe that can help. Do you have a lot of users on a slow connection and are serving large chunks of HTML? Then it could be better to use the inline technique, becasue some servers always prioritize HTML content over CSS so the user needs to download the HTML first, before the CSS is downloaded.
inlineCss.title: Inline CSS for faster first render

interactionToNextPaint.advice: No interactions were observed during this page load, so Interaction to Next Paint cannot be assessed in this snapshot. INP is best measured with real-user monitoring.
interactionToNextPaint.description: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) is one of the Google Core Web Vitals — it replaced First Input Delay in March 2024 — and measures the latency of the slowest interaction with the page. To be fast according to Google, the p75 across all interactions should be under 200 ms, and over 500 ms is poor performance. INP is best measured with real-user monitoring; this rule reports what it can observe from the events that happened during the test.
interactionToNextPaint.title: Have a fast Interaction to Next Paint

jquery.description: There are sites out there that use multiple versions of jQuery on the same page. You shouldn't do that because the user will then unnecessarily download extra data. Cleanup the code and make sure you only use one version.

largestContentfulPaint.advice: Largest contentful paint is poor 4.984 s. It is in the Google Web Vitals poor range, slower than 4 seconds.
largestContentfulPaint.description: Largest contentful paint is one of Google Web Vitals and reports the render time of the largest image or text block visible within the viewport, relative to when the page first started loading. To be fast according to Google, it needs to render before 2.5 seconds and results over 4 seconds is poor performance.
largestContentfulPaint.title: Have a fast largest contentful paint

lazyLoadingImages.advice: The page has 6 below-the-fold images without loading="lazy". Add loading="lazy" so the browser defers downloading and decoding them until the user scrolls them into view.
lazyLoadingImages.description: Adding loading="lazy" to an tells the browser not to download or decode it until it is close to the viewport. For images that the user may never see (deep in the page, behind a tab, in a footer carousel), this saves bandwidth and main-thread time during initial render. The LCP image and any image in the initial viewport should NOT be lazy-loaded — that delays the first paint. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/img#loading
lazyLoadingImages.title: Lazy-load below-the-fold images

lcpImageHints.advice: The LCP element is not an image, so this rule does not apply.
lcpImageHints.description: When the Largest Contentful Paint element is an image, the browser priority hints applied to that element directly affect the LCP metric. The image must NOT be loading="lazy" (that defers the fetch until near-viewport, which is the opposite of what an LCP image needs) and SHOULD be fetchpriority="high" (so the browser fetches it with high priority instead of guessing). https://web.dev/articles/fetch-priority
lcpImageHints.title: Apply the right priority hints to the LCP image

longTasks.advice: The page has 20 CPU long tasks with the total of 2.869 s. The total blocking time is 1.261 s  and 5 long tasks before first contentful paint with total time of 858 ms. However the CPU Long Task is depending on the computer/phones actual CPU speed, so you should measure this on the same type of the device that your user is using. Use Geckoprofiler for Firefox or Chromes tracelog to debug your long tasks.
longTasks.description: Long CPU tasks locks the thread. To the user this is commonly visible as a "locked up" page where the browser is unable to respond to user input; this is a major source of bad user experience on the web today. However the CPU Long Task is depending on the computer/phones actual CPU speed, so you should measure this on the same type of the device that your user is using. To debug you should use the Chrome timeline log and drag/drop it into devtools or use Firefox Geckoprofiler.
longTasks.title: Avoid CPU Long Tasks

modernImageFormats.advice: The page ships 12 images (out of 24) in JPEG/PNG/GIF without a modern alternative. Wrap them in a with a or "image/webp" before the legacy , or serve modern formats from your image pipeline directly. AVIF and WebP usually deliver 25–50% smaller files at the same quality.
modernImageFormats.description: AVIF and WebP routinely deliver 25–50% smaller files than JPEG and PNG at the same perceived quality, and every browser version still under support understands at least one of them. Ship modern formats either through a element with / "image/webp" entries in front of the legacy , or directly from a content-negotiating image pipeline that returns AVIF / WebP when the client accepts it. https://web.dev/articles/serve-images-webp
modernImageFormats.title: Serve images in modern formats (AVIF, WebP)

spof.advice: The page has 1 request inside of the head that can cause a SPOF (single point of failure). Load them asynchronously or move them outside of the document head.
spof.description: A page can be stopped from loading in the browser if a single JavaScript, CSS, and in some cases a font, couldn't be fetched or is loading really slowly (the white screen of death). That is a scenario you really want to avoid. Never load 3rd-party components synchronously inside of the head tag.
spof.title: Avoid Frontend single point of failures

assetsRedirects.title: Avoid doing redirects

cacheHeaders.title: Avoid extra requests by setting cache headers
cacheHeaders.description: The easiest way to make your page fast is to avoid doing requests to the server. Setting a cache header on your server response will tell the browser that it doesn't need to download the asset again during the configured cache time! Always try to set a cache time if the content doesn't change for every request.
cacheHeaders.advice: The page has 203 requests that are missing a cache time. Configure a cache time so the browser doesn't need to download them every time. It will save 2 MB the next access.

cacheHeadersLong.title: Long cache headers is good
cacheHeadersLong.description: Setting a cache header is good. Setting a long cache header (a year) is even better because the asset will stay in the browser cache across visits. For content-hashed URLs (e.g. app.4af2.css) you can safely use Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. For unversioned URLs that may change, use a revalidating strategy instead.
cacheHeadersLong.advice: The page has 35 requests that have a shorter cache time than one year (but still a cache time).

compressAssets.title: Always compress text content
compressAssets.description: In the early days of the Internet there were browsers that didn't support compressing (gzipping) text content. They do now. Make sure you compress HTML, JSON, JavaScript, CSS and SVG. It will save bytes for the user; making the page load faster and use less bandwith.
compressAssets.advice: The page has 4 requests that are served uncompressed. You could save a lot of bytes by sending them compressed instead.

There has been some hacks in the past that suggested closing the connection as fast as possible in order to create new ones, but that shouldn't be applicable anymore.

contentSecurityPolicyHeader.title: Use a strict Content-Security-Policy header to mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.description: A Content-Security-Policy response header tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed. The most effective form is a strict CSP using nonces or hashes together with strict-dynamic; the worst is a missing header, with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval close behind. https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.advice: The policy declares no default-src or script-src directive, which means scripts can be loaded from anywhere. Add at least default-src so unknown directive types fall back to a safe value. Set object-src 'none' (or a default-src 'none' fallback) so the page cannot load Flash, plugins or other legacy embeddable content.

crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header so cross-origin subresources opt in to being embedded.
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) makes the page refuse to load cross-origin subresources unless they explicitly opt in via CORP or CORS. Together with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header (typically require-corp or credentialless) on the document response to control cross-origin embedding.

crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) lets a page sever its window-group ties to cross-origin documents that opened it or that it opens. Together with Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header (typically same-origin) on the document response to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.

crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header to limit who may embed the page.
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP) is a per-response opt-in that tells the browser which origins are allowed to embed the resource. It blocks cross-origin or cross-site no-cors embedding (img, script, iframe, etc.) and is one of the building blocks of cross-origin isolation. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header (same-origin, same-site or cross-origin) on the document response to limit who may embed it.

nelHeader.title: Set a NEL header so the browser reports network errors back to you.
nelHeader.description: The NEL (Network Error Logging) response header tells the browser to record connection-level failures (DNS, TLS, HTTP errors) and ship them to a reporting endpoint. NEL pairs with the Reporting-Endpoints / Report-To header — the page declares the endpoint group and NEL points at it. Together they give you visibility into errors that never reach your origin server. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/NEL
nelHeader.advice: Set a NEL header (paired with Reporting-Endpoints) to collect connection-level error reports from the field.

permissionsPolicyHeader.title: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.
permissionsPolicyHeader.description: The Permissions-Policy response header (the successor to Feature-Policy) lets a site explicitly opt in or out of powerful browser features such as camera, microphone, geolocation, payment and clipboard. Setting a strict policy reduces the attack surface and limits what embedded third parties can do. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Permissions-Policy
permissionsPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.

referrerPolicyHeader.title: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.
referrerPolicyHeader.description: Referrer Policy is a new header that allows a site to control how much information the browser includes with navigations away from a document and should be set by all sites. https://scotthelme.co.uk/a-new-security-header-referrer-policy/.
referrerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.

reportingEndpointsHeader.title: Declare reporting endpoints so the browser can deliver Reporting-API events.
reportingEndpointsHeader.description: The Reporting-Endpoints response header (the successor to Report-To) names the URLs that browsers should POST reports to. Without it, CSP report-to directives, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have nowhere to go. The legacy Report-To header is still accepted for older Chromium versions. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Reporting-Endpoints
reportingEndpointsHeader.advice: Set a Reporting-Endpoints header (or the legacy Report-To header) so CSP reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have an endpoint to land at.

strictTransportSecurityHeader.title: Set a strict transport header to make sure the user always use HTTPS.
strictTransportSecurityHeader.description: The HTTP Strict-Transport-Security response header (often abbreviated as HSTS) lets a web site tell browsers that it should only be accessed using HTTPS, instead of using HTTP. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security.

avoidRenderBlocking.advice: The page has 3 blocking requests and 0 in body parser blocking (1 JavaScript and 2 CSS).
avoidRenderBlocking.description: The critical rendering path is what the browser needs to do to start rendering the page. Every file requested inside of the head element will postpone the rendering of the page, because the browser need to do the request. Avoid loading JavaScript synchronously inside of the head (you should not need JavaScript to render the page), request files from the same domain as the main document (to avoid DNS lookups) and inline CSS for really fast rendering and a short rendering path.
avoidRenderBlocking.title: Avoid slowing down the critical rendering path

avoidScalingImages.advice: The page has 13 images that are scaled more than 100 pixels. It would be better if those images are sent so the browser don't need to scale them.
avoidScalingImages.description: It's easy to scale images in the browser and make sure they look good in different devices, however that is bad for performance! Scaling images in the browser takes extra CPU time and will hurt performance on mobile. And the user will download extra kilobytes (sometimes megabytes) of data that could be avoided. Don't do that, make sure you create multiple version of the same image server-side and serve the appropriate one.
avoidScalingImages.title: Don't scale images in the browser

The default ("auto") leaves the choice to the browser. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/img#decoding
decodingAsync.title: Add decoding="async" to non-critical images

firstContentfulPaint.advice: First contentful paint is poor (3.644 s). It is in the Google Web Vitals poor range, slower than 3 seconds.
firstContentfulPaint.description: The First Contentful Paint (FCP) metric measures the time from when the page starts loading to when any part of the page content is rendered on the screen. For this metric, "content" refers to text, images (including background images), <svg> elements, or non-white <canvas> elements.
firstContentfulPaint.title: Have a fast first contentful paint

googleTagManager.advice: The page is using Google Tag Manager, this is a performance risk since non-tech users can add JavaScript to your page.

googleTagManager.title: Avoid using Google Tag Manager.

inlineCss.advice: The page has both inline CSS and CSS requests even though it uses a HTTP/2-ish connection. If you have many users on slow connections, it can be better to only inline the CSS. Run your own tests and check the waterfall graph to see what happens.
inlineCss.description: In the early days of the Internet, inlining CSS was one of the ugliest things you can do. That has changed if you want your page to start rendering fast for your user. Always inline the critical CSS when you use HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (avoid doing CSS requests that block rendering) and lazy load and cache the rest of the CSS. It is a little more complicated when using HTTP/2. Does your server support HTTP push? Then maybe that can help. Do you have a lot of users on a slow connection and are serving large chunks of HTML? Then it could be better to use the inline technique, becasue some servers always prioritize HTML content over CSS so the user needs to download the HTML first, before the CSS is downloaded.
inlineCss.title: Inline CSS for faster first render

interactionToNextPaint.advice: No interactions were observed during this page load, so Interaction to Next Paint cannot be assessed in this snapshot. INP is best measured with real-user monitoring.
interactionToNextPaint.description: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) is one of the Google Core Web Vitals — it replaced First Input Delay in March 2024 — and measures the latency of the slowest interaction with the page. To be fast according to Google, the p75 across all interactions should be under 200 ms, and over 500 ms is poor performance. INP is best measured with real-user monitoring; this rule reports what it can observe from the events that happened during the test.
interactionToNextPaint.title: Have a fast Interaction to Next Paint

largestContentfulPaint.advice: Largest contentful paint is poor 6.728 s. It is in the Google Web Vitals poor range, slower than 4 seconds.
largestContentfulPaint.description: Largest contentful paint is one of Google Web Vitals and reports the render time of the largest image or text block visible within the viewport, relative to when the page first started loading. To be fast according to Google, it needs to render before 2.5 seconds and results over 4 seconds is poor performance.
largestContentfulPaint.title: Have a fast largest contentful paint

lazyLoadingImages.advice: The page has 6 below-the-fold images without loading="lazy". Add loading="lazy" so the browser defers downloading and decoding them until the user scrolls them into view.
lazyLoadingImages.description: Adding loading="lazy" to an tells the browser not to download or decode it until it is close to the viewport. For images that the user may never see (deep in the page, behind a tab, in a footer carousel), this saves bandwidth and main-thread time during initial render. The LCP image and any image in the initial viewport should NOT be lazy-loaded — that delays the first paint. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/img#loading
lazyLoadingImages.title: Lazy-load below-the-fold images

lcpImageHints.advice: The LCP element is not an image, so this rule does not apply.
lcpImageHints.description: When the Largest Contentful Paint element is an image, the browser priority hints applied to that element directly affect the LCP metric. The image must NOT be loading="lazy" (that defers the fetch until near-viewport, which is the opposite of what an LCP image needs) and SHOULD be fetchpriority="high" (so the browser fetches it with high priority instead of guessing). https://web.dev/articles/fetch-priority
lcpImageHints.title: Apply the right priority hints to the LCP image

longTasks.description: Long CPU tasks locks the thread. To the user this is commonly visible as a "locked up" page where the browser is unable to respond to user input; this is a major source of bad user experience on the web today. However the CPU Long Task is depending on the computer/phones actual CPU speed, so you should measure this on the same type of the device that your user is using. modernImageFormats.advice: The page ships 11 images (out of 23) in JPEG/PNG/GIF without a modern alternative. Wrap them in a with a or "image/webp" before the legacy , or serve modern formats from your image pipeline directly. AVIF and WebP usually deliver 25–50% smaller files at the same quality.
modernImageFormats.description: AVIF and WebP routinely deliver 25–50% smaller files than JPEG and PNG at the same perceived quality, and every browser version still under support understands at least one of them. Ship modern formats either through a element with / "image/webp" entries in front of the legacy , or directly from a content-negotiating image pipeline that returns AVIF / WebP when the client accepts it. https://web.dev/articles/serve-images-webp
modernImageFormats.title: Serve images in modern formats (AVIF, WebP)

cacheHeaders.title: Avoid extra requests by setting cache headers
cacheHeaders.description: The easiest way to make your page fast is to avoid doing requests to the server. Setting a cache header on your server response will tell the browser that it doesn't need to download the asset again during the configured cache time! Always try to set a cache time if the content doesn't change for every request.

cacheHeadersLong.title: Long cache headers is good
cacheHeadersLong.description: Setting a cache header is good. Setting a long cache header (a year) is even better because the asset will stay in the browser cache across visits. For content-hashed URLs (e.g. app.4af2.css) you can safely use Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable. For unversioned URLs that may change, use a revalidating strategy instead.

referrerPolicy.advice: No <meta name="referrer"> tag was found on the page. Set a Referrer-Policy response header (preferred) or add a meta tag, for example <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">.

Set a Referrer-Policy response header (preferred) or a <meta name="referrer"> tag in the document. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy
referrerPolicy.title: Declare a referrer policy on the document

sessionReplay.description: Session-replay tools (Hotjar, FullStory, Microsoft Clarity, LogRocket, Smartlook, Mouseflow and similar) record user behaviour on the page in detail. They have legitimate uses but they have also been shown to capture personally-identifiable information from form fields when not configured with redaction. If you use one of these, make sure input redaction is on, that you have explicit user consent under the relevant regulation (GDPR, CCPA, etc.) before recording starts, and that you know where the recordings are stored and for how long. https://www.princeton.edu/~jmayer/papers/Acar2018.pdf
sessionReplay.title: Configure session-replay tools carefully if you use them

surveillance.advice: The page embeds 6 resources from companies that profit from user surveillance. Consider privacy-respecting alternatives.
surveillance.description: Embedding scripts or iframes from companies whose business model is surveillance capitalism (Google, Facebook, etc.) leaks detailed user data on every page view, often before the user has had a chance to consent. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance_capitalism for background. Prefer privacy-respecting alternatives where possible.
surveillance.title: Avoid embedding services from surveillance capitalist companies

youtube.description: If you include Youtube videos on your page, you are sharing private user information with Google.
youtube.title: Avoid including Youtube videos

contentSecurityPolicyHeader.title: Use a strict Content-Security-Policy header to mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.description: A Content-Security-Policy response header tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed. The most effective form is a strict CSP using nonces or hashes together with strict-dynamic; the worst is a missing header, with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval close behind. https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.advice: The policy declares no default-src or script-src directive, which means scripts can be loaded from anywhere. Add at least default-src so unknown directive types fall back to a safe value. Set object-src 'none' (or a default-src 'none' fallback) so the page cannot load Flash, plugins or other legacy embeddable content.

crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header so cross-origin subresources opt in to being embedded.
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) makes the page refuse to load cross-origin subresources unless they explicitly opt in via CORP or CORS. Together with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header (typically require-corp or credentialless) on the document response to control cross-origin embedding.

crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) lets a page sever its window-group ties to cross-origin documents that opened it or that it opens. crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header to limit who may embed the page.

It blocks cross-origin or cross-site no-cors embedding (img, script, iframe, etc.) and is one of the building blocks of cross-origin isolation. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header (same-origin, same-site or cross-origin) on the document response to limit who may embed it.

nelHeader.title: Set a NEL header so the browser reports network errors back to you.

NEL pairs with the Reporting-Endpoints / Report-To header — the page declares the endpoint group and NEL points at it. Together they give you visibility into errors that never reach your origin server. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/NEL

permissionsPolicyHeader.title: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.

reportingEndpointsHeader.advice: Set a Reporting-Endpoints header (or the legacy Report-To header) so CSP reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have an endpoint to land at.

inlineCss.advice: The page has both inline CSS and CSS requests even though it uses a HTTP/2-ish connection. If you have many users on slow connections, it can be better to only inline the CSS. Run your own tests and check the waterfall graph to see what happens.
inlineCss.description: In the early days of the Internet, inlining CSS was one of the ugliest things you can do. That has changed if you want your page to start rendering fast for your user. Always inline the critical CSS when you use HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (avoid doing CSS requests that block rendering) and lazy load and cache the rest of the CSS. It is a little more complicated when using HTTP/2. Does your server support HTTP push? Then maybe that can help. Do you have a lot of users on a slow connection and are serving large chunks of HTML? Then it could be better to use the inline technique, becasue some servers always prioritize HTML content over CSS so the user needs to download the HTML first, before the CSS is downloaded.

If you use one of these, make sure input redaction is on, that you have explicit user consent under the relevant regulation (GDPR, CCPA, etc.) before recording starts, and that you know where the recordings are stored and for how long. https://www.princeton.edu/~jmayer/papers/Acar2018.pdf

contentSecurityPolicyHeader.title: Use a strict Content-Security-Policy header to mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.description: A Content-Security-Policy response header tells the browser which sources of script, style, and other content are allowed. The most effective form is a strict CSP using nonces or hashes together with strict-dynamic; the worst is a missing header, with unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval close behind. https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
contentSecurityPolicyHeader.advice: The policy declares no default-src or script-src directive, which means scripts can be loaded from anywhere. Add at least default-src so unknown directive types fall back to a safe value. Set object-src 'none' (or a default-src 'none' fallback) so the page cannot load Flash, plugins or other legacy embeddable content.

crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header so cross-origin subresources opt in to being embedded.
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) makes the page refuse to load cross-origin subresources unless they explicitly opt in via CORP or CORS. Together with Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
crossOriginEmbedderPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header (typically require-corp or credentialless) on the document response to control cross-origin embedding.

crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) lets a page sever its window-group ties to cross-origin documents that opened it or that it opens. Together with Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy it puts the page in a cross-origin isolated context, which mitigates cross-window side-channel attacks (Spectre) and unlocks high-resolution timers and SharedArrayBuffer. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy
crossOriginOpenerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header (typically same-origin) on the document response to isolate the page from cross-origin windows.

crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.title: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header to limit who may embed the page.
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.description: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP) is a per-response opt-in that tells the browser which origins are allowed to embed the resource. It blocks cross-origin or cross-site no-cors embedding (img, script, iframe, etc.) and is one of the building blocks of cross-origin isolation. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy
crossOriginResourcePolicyHeader.advice: Set a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header (same-origin, same-site or cross-origin) on the document response to limit who may embed it.

googleReCaptcha.title: Avoid using Google reCAPTCHA
googleReCaptcha.description: You should avoid using Google reCAPTCHA since it will share your users information with Google.

mixedContent.title: Serve all responses on HTTPS (when you are on HTTPS)
mixedContent.description: You need to make sure that if you are on HTTPS, all responses are on HTTPS so that the content served are secured.

nelHeader.title: Set a NEL header so the browser reports network errors back to you.
nelHeader.description: The NEL (Network Error Logging) response header tells the browser to record connection-level failures (DNS, TLS, HTTP errors) and ship them to a reporting endpoint. NEL pairs with the Reporting-Endpoints / Report-To header — the page declares the endpoint group and NEL points at it. Together they give you visibility into errors that never reach your origin server. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/NEL
nelHeader.advice: Set a NEL header (paired with Reporting-Endpoints) to collect connection-level error reports from the field.

permissionsPolicyHeader.title: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.
permissionsPolicyHeader.description: The Permissions-Policy response header (the successor to Feature-Policy) lets a site explicitly opt in or out of powerful browser features such as camera, microphone, geolocation, payment and clipboard. Setting a strict policy reduces the attack surface and limits what embedded third parties can do. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Permissions-Policy
permissionsPolicyHeader.advice: Set a Permissions-Policy header to control which browser features the page can use.

referrerPolicyHeader.title: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.
referrerPolicyHeader.description: Referrer Policy is a new header that allows a site to control how much information the browser includes with navigations away from a document and should be set by all sites. https://scotthelme.co.uk/a-new-security-header-referrer-policy/.
referrerPolicyHeader.advice: Set a referrer-policy header to make sure you do not leak user information.

reportingEndpointsHeader.title: Declare reporting endpoints so the browser can deliver Reporting-API events.
reportingEndpointsHeader.description: The Reporting-Endpoints response header (the successor to Report-To) names the URLs that browsers should POST reports to. Without it, CSP report-to directives, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have nowhere to go. The legacy Report-To header is still accepted for older Chromium versions. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Reporting-Endpoints
reportingEndpointsHeader.advice: Set a Reporting-Endpoints header (or the legacy Report-To header) so CSP reports, NEL data and other Reporting-API events have an endpoint to land at.

strictTransportSecurityHeader.title: Set a strict transport header to make sure the user always use HTTPS.
strictTransportSecurityHeader.description: The HTTP Strict-Transport-Security response header (often abbreviated as HSTS) lets a web site tell browsers that it should only be accessed using HTTPS, instead of using HTTP. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security.

inlineCss.advice: The page has both inline CSS and CSS requests even though it uses a HTTP/2-ish connection. If you have many users on slow connections, it can be better to only inline the CSS. Run your own tests and check the waterfall graph to see what happens.
inlineCss.description: In the early days of the Internet, inlining CSS was one of the ugliest things you can do. That has changed if you want your page to start rendering fast for your user. Always inline the critical CSS when you use HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 (avoid doing CSS requests that block rendering) and lazy load and cache the rest of the CSS. It is a little more complicated when using HTTP/2. Does your server support HTTP push? Then maybe that can help. Do you have a lot of users on a slow connection and are serving large chunks of HTML? Then it could be better to use the inline technique, becasue some servers always prioritize HTML content over CSS so the user needs to download the HTML first, before the CSS is downloaded.
inlineCss.title: Inline CSS for faster first render
